# Digest R6 — 2 Pet 2:1–16 (L2888–3234)

**Source:** Gene L. Green, *Jude and 2 Peter* (BECNT)  
**Cache:** `R6-2pet-2_1-16.txt`  
**Range read:** L2888–3234  
**Tags:** `2-peter`, `jude`, `gene-green`, `2-peter-jude-relationship`, `balaam`, `noah`, `lot`, `green-jude-2peter-becnt`

## Coverage

Full sequential read of Green’s exegesis of **2 Peter 2:1–16**: translation block and verse-by-verse comments for 2:1–3 (false teachers); unit introduction and exegesis of 2:4–10a (OT judgment/salvation examples: angels, flood/Noah, Sodom/Lot; apodosis 2:9–10a); unit introduction and exegesis of 2:10b–16 (vices; Balaam typology); Additional Notes on textual variants at 2:4, 2:6, 2:11, 2:13, 2:14, 2:15.  
**Not claimed:** material outside this cache range; Green’s full “Opponents” / “Relationship between 2 Peter and Jude” intro essays (only cross-references as they appear in-range).

---

## Claims

### 2:1–3 false teachers among you

1. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: 2:1 is the first direct naming of the opponents after groundwork against their charges.  
   Quote: “For the first time in the letter, Peter directly addresses the problem of the heretics. … But not until 2:1 does he turn to name the opponents who were troubling the church.” (L2894)

2. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: “false prophets” are those who speak on their own, not for God—linking to 1:19–21.  
   Quote: ““False prophets” are those who speak on their own and do not speak for God (see 1:20–21 and comments).” (L2894)

3. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: ancient false prophets act “among the people” = Israel; typologically prefigure the Christian community and coming false teachers.  
   Quote: “The ancient people prefigure the Christian community, as the ancient false prophets are a sign of the coming false teachers.” (L2898)

4. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: ψευδοδιδάσκαλοι is unique to 2 Pet 2:1 in NT/LXX; *pseudo* marks both false claim and erroneous teaching.  
   Quote: “Ψευδοδιδάσκαλοι (pseudodidaskaloi) is a unique term for Peter, found only here in the NT and LXX.” (L2900)  
   Quote: “Pseudo here “suggests both that the claim of the men concerned is false and also that their teaching is erroneous…”” (L2916)

5. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: future “there will be” (2:1–3; 3:3) coexists with present arrival (feasting, seeking converts, perverting Paul); not explained by preserved apostolic prophecy-quote form as in Jude.  
   Quote: “It may be, as Moo (1996: 92) suggests, that Peter is quoting earlier apostolic prophecies here and in so doing preserves the future tense (cf. Jude 17–18 and comments). Unlike Jude, however, 2 Peter offers the readers no indication that former prophecies are being quoted.” (L2918)

6. **[false-teacher profile]** Green rejects pseudepigraphical “testament prediction” as explanation of the futures.  
   Quote: “This explanation is unable to account for the shift to the present tense in the following verses, however, and rests on a foundation no stronger than the supposed ineptitude of the pseudepigrapher.” (L2920)

7. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: present/future oscillation is eschatological—heretics come in last days; their presence shows last times have come.  
   Quote: “The oscillation between the present and the future in the letter in reference to the heretics appears to be rooted in the author’s eschatology. The heretics will come in the last days (3:3–4), and their presence in the church is evidence that the last times have come (3:5–7).” (L2922)

8. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: παρεισάξουσιν does **not** mean secret stealth (contra NIV “secretly introduce”) but simply “brought in.”  
   Quote: “While the majority of the translations suggest that these people use stealth tactics (as the NIV rendering, “They will secretly introduce destructive heresies”), the term does not evoke the concept of secrecy or malicious intent but simply that something will be “brought in”…” (L2924)

9. **[2-peter-jude-relationship] [false-teacher profile]** Green: language similar to Jude 4 (dependence) but thought not identical—Jude’s “weaseled their way in” vs Peter’s introducing heresies.  
   Quote: “Although Peter’s language is similar to Jude 4, a verse on which he is dependent, his thought is not identical to Jude, who says of the heretics, “For certain men have weaseled their way in” (see comments).” (L2926)

10. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: αἱρέσεις in 2:1 is pejorative heterodox doctrine; church and heresy are material opposites.  
    Quote: “But in 2 Pet. 2:1 the author uses it in a pejorative sense: it points to the heretics’ heterodox doctrine… In other words, “ἐκκλησία [ekklēsia, church] and αἵρεσις [hairesis, faction/heresy] are material opposites…”” (L2926)

11. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: heresy’s nature—denies coming of Lord and future judgment; libertine morality; rupture with apostolic/prophetic heritage; doctrinal + ethical + social; ends in destruction.  
    Quote: “Principally, it denied the coming of the Lord and future judgment, and this theological perspective was joined with a libertine morality (2:14, 18–19; 3:3–9), as well as a rupture with the apostolic and prophetic heritage (1:16–21). … The error had doctrinal, ethical, and social components…” (L2928)

12. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: genitive “of destruction” is objective (end = final doom), not mere quality “destructive.”  
    Quote: “The genitive “of destruction” does not simply mean that the heresies are “destructive” but also that their end is this final doom (objective genitive, not genitive of quality; BDF §163).” (L2928)

13. **[2-peter-jude-relationship] [false-teacher profile]** Green: 2 Peter’s heresy should not be identified with Jude’s, though contours similar; Peter modifies Jude 4—drops “alter grace… into sexual excess,” omits “only… Lord, Jesus Christ,” adds Master “bought them.”  
    Quote: “Although the heresy that 2 Peter addresses should not be identified with what Jude denounces, they share some similar contours. For that reason, Peter picks up and modifies the language of Jude 4… Peter has dropped the note saying that the heretics “alter the grace of our God into sexual excess” and omits “only . . . Lord, Jesus Christ,” and adds that the Master has “bought them.”” (L2930)

14. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: “deny the Master who bought them” evokes slave manumission; heretics repudiate the one who freed them—shock and audacity.  
    Quote: “The language evokes the image of the manumission of slaves (Deissmann 1911: 322–27). … Yet the heretics have repudiated the very one who freed them, the Master. The denunciation has shock effect and highlights the audacity of the heretics.” (L2932–2934)

15. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: ταχινήν = soon-coming (imminent), not merely sudden; holds delay and speed together (“paratactical thinking”); challenges “early catholic” fading parousia hope.  
    Quote: “he holds to the notion that the final judgment is imminent or “soon-coming” (ταχινήν, tachinēn… The author’s affirmation brings into question the view that the letter belongs to a supposed “early catholic” period when the hope of the parousia had faded from view. Peter expects that judgment will come swiftly, even though delay is involved (3:8–10).” (L2938)

16. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: impact twofold—(a) many follow licentious deeds (antidiscipleship); (b) way of truth blasphemed, hindering mission.  
    Quote: “The impact of the heretics on the Christian community is twofold: they persuade those in the church to follow their error (2:2a), and since they are associated with the church, their conduct fuels the fires of dissent against the gospel and hinders Christian mission (2:2b).” (L2940)

17. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: ἀσελγείαις = libertine/outrageous conduct, often sexual; sexual license distinguishing mark of the heresy; appeal resonates with pagan sexual mores.  
    Quote: “Sexual license is a distinguishing mark of their heresy (2:10, 12, 14; 3:3). … The heretics’ appeal, on the other hand, resonated with the sexual mores of the street.” (L2950)

18. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: “way of truth” = lifestyle not only beliefs; equivalent to “straight way” (2:15) and “way of righteousness” (2:21); conduct so bad even wider society objects.  
    Quote: “Since their conduct has generated such antipathy, we can surmise that they have engaged in behavior that is not even acceptable according to the norms of the wider society (cf. 1 Cor. 5:1). … The description of the Christian faith as “the way of truth” underscores how the apostle views it as a lifestyle and not only as a set of beliefs.” (L2954)

19. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: greed + πλαστοῖς λόγοις (“pretensions,” not fables) + ἐμπορεύσονται (exploit/misrepresent merchandise)—sophist-like peddling; charge of greed not empty vituperatio because developed through the fabric.  
    Quote: “Although the charge of “greed” was a commonplace in vituperatio (L. Johnson 1989: 430), the author’s development of the theme through the fabric of his accusation suggests that such exploitation was actually going on. … Deception is at the heart of their persuasive appeal.” (L2960–2962)

20. **[2-peter-jude-relationship] [false-teacher profile]** Green: “judgment is not delayed for a long time” reworks Jude 4’s “from long ago marked out for this judgment”—drops proscribed-from-ancient-times; counters delay argument and Epicurean-style delay = no judgment.  
    Quote: “Peter’s declaration is a reworking of Jude 4: … Our author has left to one side the notion of a judgment that was proscribed from ancient times as he hones the affirmation to respond more precisely to the heretics’ claims. Though the language is similar (note the substitution of ἔκπαλαι, ekpalai, for πάλαι, palai), the thought is not exactly the same.” (L2968)  
    Quote: “Perhaps more significant than the author’s source is the way this counterpoint arrests the widely known Epicurean notion that the delay in divine judgment means that no judgment is coming…” (L2970)

21. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: destruction “does not slumber” personifies final judgment; delay ≠ idle; inclusio with 2:1b; past judgment prefigures future (next unit).  
    Quote: “In this metaphor, final destruction is personified and is said not to be dozing or slumbering: it is on its way… His argument here is that destruction will come, a point he develops in the following verses by showing how in the past God certainly did execute his judgment.” (L2974)

### 2:4–10a OT examples (angels, flood, Sodom)

22. **[noah] [lot] [2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green: 2:4–10a one long conditional (protasis 4–8; apodosis 9–10a); refutes claim God never intervenes and that judgment would sweep the righteous; examples in chronological order: sinful angels, flood world, Sodom/Gomorrah; deliverance of Noah (+ family) and Lot.  
    Quote: “Their claim is that there is no evidence that God intervenes to judge the world, either in the past or present, and therefore he will not judge humanity in the future. … He forwards as examples the sinful angels (v. 4), the ancient world of the flood generation (v. 5), and the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah (v. 6)… At the same time, Peter demonstrates that God delivered the righteous during two of these judgments, forwarding the examples of Noah and his family (v. 5) along with Lot (vv. 7–8).” (L2982)

23. **[2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green: litany draws principally on Jude 5–8 but different selection and purpose—Jude: exodus generation, fallen angels, Sodom (privileged status no exemption); Peter: reality of judgment **and** preservation.  
    Quote: “Jude’s choice, however, is somewhat different from Peter’s as he names the exodus generation, the fallen angels, and the Sodom and Gomorrah stories as his types. … Peter, however, strings together these texts for a different purpose, that being to affirm the reality of divine judgment as well as divine preservation. The problems these authors face are not identical and their responses, though similar, are constructed to affirm different points.” (L2984)

24. **[2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green: angels (2:4)—source Jude 6 but truncated; Jude stresses apostasy/deserting domain as type of invaders; Peter stresses certainty of judgment (“sinned” only).  
    Quote: “Peter has truncated Jude’s more-elaborate description of the angelic sin… Jude’s primary focus, however, is on the angelic apostasy… Peter, on the other hand, is principally interested in the question of the certainty of divine judgment… Therefore… Peter simply mentions they had “sinned”…” (L3005)

25. **[2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green: angelic-fall traditions from Gen 6:1–4 / Watchers; **no direct reference to 1 Enoch** in 2 Peter (contrast Jude 14–15).  
    Quote: “There is, however, no direct reference to 1 Enoch either here or elsewhere in 2 Peter (cf. Jude 14–15 and comments).” (L3007)

26. **[2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green: echoes Jude 6b (kept for judgment; chains/darkness) but adds ταρταρώσας—handed over to Tartarus; God as judicial actor; angels kept as type/guarantee of future judgment of ungodly.  
    Quote: “Peter notes that instead of sparing the angels who sinned (2:4a), God handed them (implied object) over (παρέδωκεν, paredōken). … Peter qualifies that by this divine judicial act they were “sent . . . to the underworld” (ταρταρώσας, tartarōsas). … The way he kept the angels for this judgment becomes both a type of God’s judicial action toward the godless and a guarantee that the future judgment will certainly come.” (L3011, L3015)

27. **[noah] [2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green: flood example (2:5) **not dependent on Jude** (Jude omits flood generation); stands in Jewish catalogs linking Watchers, flood, Sodom.  
    Quote: “At this point, Peter is not dependent on Jude since Jude does not refer to the flood generation in his catalog of ancient sinners… Second Peter 2:4–8 stands, as does Jude, within this broad interpretive tradition that connects the angelic fall, human sin, and divine judgment…” (L3019)

28. **[noah]** Green: 2 Pet 2:5 likely adapts 1 Pet 3:19–20 (angelic fall + flood + “eight”; saved/kept; flood; sinful era)—handling similar to adoption/modification of Jude.  
    Quote: “But as already noted, both texts join together the tradition of the angelic fall with the flood as well as mentioning the “eight” who were spared the flood. … Our author’s handling of this text from 1 Peter is strikingly similar to the way he adopts and modifies the thought and language of Jude… The multiple conceptual similarities between the two texts secure the case.” (L3023)

29. **[noah]** Green: “ancient world” = flood-generation humanity; flood type of future fire judgment (3:5–7); God “kept” Noah as herald of righteousness + seven others.  
    Quote: “Peter sees this destruction as the type of the future judgment by fire (3:5–7).” (L3025)  
    Quote: “Peter comments that Noah was a preacher or “herald of righteousness” (δικαιοσύνης κήρυκα, dikaiosynēs kēryka)… yet nowhere in the OT is he described as preacher or herald… of the message of justice. … But Jewish and Christian literature refers to Noah’s proclamation to sinners of his day…” (L3029)

30. **[noah]** Green: few saved under Noah’s preaching is grim reminder for readers tempted by heretics; future judgment by fire not water.  
    Quote: “Although he preached, few were saved, a grim reminder for Peter’s readers, who were tempted by the heretics’ persuasion. … Yet the coming judgment will not be by water as in the flood, but by fire (3:5–7).” (L3029, L3031)

31. **[lot] [2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green: Sodom (2:6) returns to Jude 7 but modifies heavily—drops surrounding cities’ detail and “another kind of flesh”; focuses on judgment as prototype, not sin description; ὑπόδειγμα vs Jude’s δεῖγμα; reduced to ashes vs “penalty of eternal fire.”  
    Quote: “Peter returns to Jude as his source (Jude 7 and comments), yet modifying the text of Jude significantly in the direction of his own purposes. … Peter shows little interest in the description of the sins of these cities since his primary purpose is to underscore their judgment, which serves as a prototype of future judgment.” (L3035)

32. **[lot]** Green: Sodom/Gomorrah as sample of ungodly doom; residual remnant typology (Lot) links to final judgment deliverance.  
    Quote: “We might say that the doom of Sodom and Gomorrah was just a sample of things to come.” (L3043)  
    Quote: “The typology of the Lot story becomes a primary argument in Peter’s refutation of the heretics.” (L3045)

33. **[lot]** Green: “righteous Lot” not stated in Genesis; echoes Wis 10:6 language; righteousness thematic vs heretics’ unrighteousness; ambiguities of Lot acknowledged but Peter does not explore them—point is God spares righteous, judges wicked.  
    Quote: “Lot’s story is juxtaposed with that of Noah… Genesis never states that Lot was “righteous.” Wisdom 10:6 reflects not only the thought but also the language…” (L3045–3047)  
    Quote: “Peter’s concern in the present passage does not take him deep into the moral dilemma of the Lot story. His point is that in the time of divine judgment, God spares the righteous while executing his judgment on the wicked (2 Pet. 2:5–9).” (L3053)

34. **[lot] [false-teacher profile]** Green: καταπονούμενον = threatened violence/oppression (Gen 19:9), not first mental distress (that is v. 8); suggests heretics act aggressively as oppressive force.  
    Quote: “It is not mental distress that is referred to here—that comes in ver. 8—but the threatened violence of Gen 19.9” (MM 331, cited). “Peter’s mention of this harassment and oppression suggests that the heretics themselves are acting aggressively…” (L3055)

35. **[lot] [false-teacher profile]** Green: Sodomites’ “licentious way of life of the lawless” typologically linked to heretics (ἀσέλγεια also of heretics 2:2, 18); sexual orientation of sin suggested without specifics.  
    Quote: “Later in the chapter, Peter underscores the moral lawlessness of the heretics as they aggressively seek disciples, thus drawing a typological line between them and the inhabitants of Sodom (3:17).” (L3057)  
    Quote: “Without drawing out the specifics, the author suggests that the Sodomites’ sin, as that of the heretics, had a sexual orientation.” (L3059)

36. **[lot]** Green: 2:8—Lot day after day sees/hears lawless deeds; torments righteous soul (inner reaction preferred); continuous way of life, not one incident—prefigures depth of heretics’ moral decay.  
    Quote: “The picture is not simply of an individual act but of a way of life (2:7) that produces such actions. … Insofar as these prefigure the heretics, Peter highlights the depth of their moral decay.” (L3065)

37. **[noah] [lot]** Green: apodosis 2:9—Lord “knows how” = ability to deliver devout from trial and keep unrighteous for day of judgment; εὐσεβεῖς vs ἄδικοι/ἀσεβεῖς; trials include eschatological (with present testing as part of final trial).  
    Quote: “Peter’s declaration that God “knows” (οἶδεν, oiden) how to deliver the devout is not a simple statement about his cognition but rather a declaration of his ability…” (L3067)  
    Quote: “the eschatological reference to the “day of judgment” in the second half of the verse suggests that Peter has eschatological trials in view here as well… with the present testing being part of that final trial the church will endure…” (L3071)

38. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: present participle κολαζομένους read as future-oriented final-judgment torment (not current/interim only); doom is enduring torment, not annihilation.  
    Quote: “The eschatological orientation of the passage… suggests that Peter has in view the torment that the unrighteous will experience at that time. … Their doom is sure, and their end is torment that will endure, not annihilation.” (L3081)

39. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: God’s dual powers—save and judge—affirmed against heretics’ denials (possibly Epicurean transcendence precluding both); Philo parallel on beneficent and punitive powers.  
    Quote: “The heretics have denied God’s power to judge (3:3–7). Apparently doubts have arisen about God’s ability to save as well. If the heretics have absorbed aspects of Epicurean teaching… then their doctrine of divine transcendence precludes both of these. … Peter affirms them both in the face of the heretics’ denials.” (L3083)

40. **[2-peter-jude-relationship] [false-teacher profile]** Green: 2:10a adapts Jude 7–8, 16 complexly—drops “another kind of flesh”; “go after flesh” = sexual gratification devotion; “defiling desire”; “disdain lordship” (κυριότητος) = Christ’s ruling authority, not plural angelic κυριότητες; links to 2:1 deny Master.  
    Quote: “Peter is hardly a slave to Jude’s language and thought as he adopts and adapts his source… The level of modification would have exempted Peter from the charge of theft…” (L3089)  
    Quote: “Here, as in Jude 8… the author refers to the ruling power of the Lord (κύριος, kyrios), who is Jesus Christ… The heretics are people who “disdain” his ruling authority, a statement that takes up again Peter’s previous accusation that the false teachers “deny the Master who bought them” (2:1).” (L3097)

### 2:10b–16 vices; Balaam

41. **[false-teacher profile] [balaam] [2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green (unit intro): 2:10b–16 denounces arrogance, irrationality, pleasure, sexual enticement, greed; Balaam typology (sex + greed as means to tempt); **highly dependent on Jude 10–12** but reworked significantly for Peter’s heretics.  
    Quote: “Peter’s denunciation of the heretics is highly dependent on Jude 10–12 (see comments). But Peter reworks this material significantly as he tailors it to address the heretics that trouble the churches.” (L3116)

42. **[2-peter-jude-relationship] [false-teacher profile]** Green: 2:10b—τολμηταί suggested by Jude 9’s verb (what Michael did **not** do); adds they “show no fear” when blaspheming “glories”; omits Michael/Moses/devil legend but keeps slandering angels.  
    Quote: “The use of this term was suggested to the author by the presence of the verb in Jude 9… Jude 8 simply states δόξας δὲ βλασφημοῦσιν… while Peter adds that the heretics do not tremble… Peter omits the legend about Michael’s contention with the devil over the body of Moses (Jude 9) but preserves the reference to slandering angels, that is, “glories”…” (L3127–3129)

43. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: “glories” = angelic beings (not civil/ecclesiastical authorities); reason for blasphemy differs from Jude—Jude: reject divine order angels guard; 2 Peter: deny providence/judgment, linked to angels’ role in final assize; not fallen angels.  
    Quote: “In that letter, the heretics have rejected the divine order of things, of which the angels are guardians. However, the heretics in Peter’s sights have denied providence and divine judgment… We may assume that their rejection of angelic authority is linked to the common understanding of the angelic role in the execution of the final judgment… These are not the “fallen angels” (contra Bauckham 1983: 261) but those who accompany the Lord in the great assize…” (L3133)

44. **[2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green: 2:11 transforms Jude 9—drops apocryphal Michael/devil/Moses story; Michael → angels “greater in strength and power”; “judgment of slander” → “slanderous judgment”; “Lord punish you” → do not bring charge “before the Lord.”  
    Quote: “Peter has altogether dropped the reference to the apocryphal story of the contention between the archangel Michael and the devil over the body of Moses… Instead, he substitutes the reference to Michael with the “angels,” who themselves are “greater in strength and power.”” (L3135)  
    Quote: “Our author is reluctant to integrate the apocryphal traditions as did Jude yet retains some of their significant concepts, while altering even these in notable ways.” (L3137)

45. **[2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green: adaptation = ancient *imitatio*—make borrowed material one’s own; not ignorance of source, not reader-unfamiliarity, not anti-Scripture of apocrypha; Perkins: omit because not relevant to argument.  
    Quote: “Peter’s intertextual methodology has truly transformed Jude’s thought, making it his own to advance his purposes. What he means is not bound by his source’s intent. His mode of adapting his source material is in line with ancient canons of imitatio, which allowed borrowed material to be reworked extensively to make it one’s own.” (L3139)

46. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: angels’ restraint from “slanderous judgment” before the Lord models nobility against honor-culture revenge for hubris; legal language (charge against them).  
    Quote: “The angels, though in a superior position and able to enact litigation against their inferiors, show great nobility of character in their restraint by not bringing a “slanderous judgment” against their opponents.” (L3145)

47. **[2-peter-jude-relationship] [false-teacher profile]** Green: 2:12 from Jude 10—keeps “irrational beasts” and slandering what they don’t understand; twists instinct-knowledge → nature born to capture/destroy; moral corruption → final destruction; Jude: corrupt character; Peter: final destiny vs denial of judgment.  
    Quote: “Whereas the emphasis in Jude 10 is on the corrupt character of the heretics, Peter’s principal concern is with their final destiny. Once again, our author has adopted and adapted his source in a way that speaks directly to the situation at hand.” (L3149)

48. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: “destroyed in their destruction” = share beasts’ slaughter-destiny (αὐτῶν = animals), not “utterly perish in their own corruption” (NKJV/Semitic idiom) and not evil angels.  
    Quote: “The topic of the present verse is the destruction of the animals, and these beasts are the immediate and logical antecedent to “their.” … The heretics will be destroyed in the final assize as beasts who are captured and killed.” (L3157)

49. **[2-peter-jude-relationship] [balaam] [false-teacher profile]** Green: 2:13 partly from Jude 11–12—μισθόν from Balaam “for gain”; feasting with you (συνευωχούμενοι); drops fearless + ἀγάπαις; plays ἀπάταις (“pleasures”); compounds σπίλοι καὶ μῶμοι; conscious modification not memory lapse.  
    Quote: “It is unlikely that this subtle engineering of his source is due to our author’s lapse in memory as he seeks to recall what he read sometime in Jude but rather suggests that he was engaged in a conscious modification of Jude’s thought as he made it his own and applied it to this new situation…” (L3161)

50. **[balaam] [false-teacher profile]** Green: “suffering the loss of the wages of unrighteousness” = gain from wickedness ends as loss; sets up Balaam comparison (2:15); avarice charge returns.  
    Quote: “By referring to the heretics’ μισθὸν ἀδικίας… Peter is setting up the comparison between the heretics and Balaam (2:15). … As in the case of Balaam, profit is one of their driving motivations…” (L3165)

51. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: daytime reveling as scandal (night = expected time of debauchery); pleasure-seeking contrasted with Jewish/Christian teaching; later Epicurean “rotted fruits” critique framed via Lactantius (not that heretics are pure Epicurus).  
    Quote: “The scandal of the heretics’ lifestyle is that they even engage in such living “in the daytime”… Therefore it was particularly scandalous to participate in these activities during the daytime… Their lack of public shame is astounding.” (L3173)

52. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: heretics feast with the church, transforming Lord’s Supper context into pagan-style revelry/symposion sensuality.  
    Quote: “The heretics Peter combats have transformed the Christian celebration into an event marked by cultural practices that are antithetical to authentic Christian feasting. … They approach the Lord’s Supper as they would any pagan feast.” (L3177, L3179)

53. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: 2:14—eyes full of adulteress; **not dependent on Jude** here; echoes Jesus’ adultery-of-heart teaching (Matt 5:28) and wider moralists; unceasing sin is sexual; fishing metaphor “luring unstable people” with (implied sexual) bait.  
    Quote: “Peter’s denunciation does not depend on Jude either at this point or in the rest of the verse. We suspect, however, that he echoes the teaching of Jesus about the source of sexual sin…” (L3181)  
    Quote: “His present discussion about the sexual vice of the heretics suggests that the enticement in mind in 2:14 is sexual as well.” (L3189)

54. **[false-teacher profile]** Green: “hearts trained in greed”—gymnasium metaphor of training turned to vice; couples sex and money as Balaam enticed Israel; “cursed children” = under divine curse/judgment they deny; irony; Balaam story’s unpronounceable curse inverted.  
    Quote: “The heretics demonstrate a pattern of exploitation that couples sex and money in the same way as Balaam enticed Israel (see 2:15–16 and comments).” (L3193)  
    Quote: “The very verdict that the heretics have denied would ever be pronounced is on them… The irony in this revelation is thick.” (L3195)

55. **[balaam] [2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green: 2:15 compresses Jude 11’s triple Cain/Balaam/Korah to **Balaam only**; “way of Balaam of Bosor” replaces “way of Cain”; heretics “wandered off” (apostasy) vs Jude’s “error”; fuller Balaam typology.  
    Quote: “In singling out only Balaam, Peter compresses the triple denunciation of Cain, Balaam, and Korah from his source, Jude 11… Although Peter draws on the Balaam story as suggested by Jude, his development of the typology is much fuller as he echoes the wider Balaam traditions.” (L3197)

56. **[balaam] [false-teacher profile]** Green: departing straight way = willful apostasy; following Balaam’s way = antidiscipleship; Balaam known for greed + counseling sexual seduction of Israel; heretics same practice.  
    Quote: “When Balaam thought his hope for gain was lost, he encouraged Balak to entice Israel to sexual sin… The heretics engage in the same practice. Peter’s warning against the heretics cannot be more dire. They, too, entice others to sexual sin and are motivated by greed (2:14, 18).” (L3203)

57. **[balaam] [2-peter-jude-relationship]** Green: 2:16 goes **well beyond Jude**—donkey story absent from Jude; legal accusation for unlawful deed; donkey (not only angel as in Num 22:31–35) restrains prophet; closer to targums/Josephus than plain Numbers.  
    Quote: “In drawing the line between the heretics and Balaam, Peter goes well beyond Jude’s recounting of the Balaam story, recalling contours of the tradition that Jude left to one side…” (L3205)  
    Quote: “His use of the Balaam story is closer to the targums than to Num. 22:31–35, which identifies the Angel of the Lord as the one who accuses Balaam of acting perversely.” (L3207)

58. **[balaam] [false-teacher profile]** Green: speechless donkey speaks with human voice; ironic contrast with irrational/mad prophet; Balaam called “prophet” (not Numbers’ term)—eye on heretics’ claim of divine authority (2:1); heretics share Balaam’s παραφρονία—why heed them?  
    Quote: “Peter appears to be setting up the deeply ironic contrast between the dumb ass, who speaks rationally, and the prophet Balaam, who is mad or irrational.” (L3209)  
    Quote: “Peter likely has one eye fixed on the heretics, who themselves claim divine authority for their views (2:1). Previously in this paragraph Peter has compared them to “irrational beasts” (2:12), and now in a similar way they are compared with the prophet Balaam’s “irrationality”… The heretics follow in Balaam’s way (2 Pet. 2:15). Why should anyone heed them?” (L3211)

### Jude parallels / imitatio notes

### Additional Notes

72. **Text 2:4:** Green prefers σειραῖς (“chains”) over σιροῖς/σειροῖς (“pit/cave”) given dependence on Jude 6 δεσμοῖς.  
    Quote: “Peter’s dependence on Jude 6—which reads δεσμοῖς (desmois, chains)—suggests that our author has included the synonym σειραῖς (seirais, chains). This reading is probably the most ancient.” (L3104)

73. **Text 2:6:** καταστροφῇ bracketed; may be omitted by transcriptional oversight (two κατ- words). ἀσεβέσιν preferred over ἀσεβεῖν. (L3106–3108)

74. **Text 2:11:** παρὰ κυρίῳ (dative) preferred for inclusion with strong attestation; genitive harder but dative better supported in Green’s discussion. (L3216)

75. **Text 2:13:** ἀδικούμενοι strongly attested vs κομιούμενοι (easier “receiving wages”). (L3218)

76. **Text 2:14:** μοιχαλίδος (adulteress) hardest/best supported vs μοιχείας/μοιχαλίας. (L3220)

77. **[balaam] Text 2:15 Bosor:** Βοσόρ more difficult/better attested than harmonizing Βεώρ; Green surveys (a) “son of flesh” play (unparalleled/unclear to readers), (b) place-name Bosor/Aram region from someone knowing Balaam geography, (c) Hays: tradition-history confusion with Edomite king-lists / Bezer.  
    Quote: “What appears to some as “‘Peter’s’ mistake” (Kelly 1969: 343) could, in fact, come from someone who knew the region and the whole Balaam story quite well.” (L3222)
